given: Mean = sum of fx over sum of f
Standard deviation = square root of (sum of f x squared over sum of f, minus the mean squared)

mustKnow: For a plain list, sum of f is n, so the formula reads sum of x squared over n minus the mean squared
Square each value before adding: sum of x squared is not the square of the total
The bracket under the root is the variance; take the root for the standard deviation
The calculator's sigma key divides by n; its s key divides by n minus 1

Calculate the mean and keep it unrounded for the next step
Substitute into $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \bar{x}^{2}}$ and finish with the square root
Tell the variance apart from the standard deviation and give whichever is asked for

sheet.howExamined: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. The standard deviation of a raw list is set as a part of 3 to 5 marks: Summer 2025 Q2 was a single 5-mark part (the mean M1 W1, then MW1 M1 W1 for the standard deviation) and Summer 2023 Q6(i) was 3 marks (MW1 for the mean, W1 for the sum of squares, MW1 for the answer). Most papers since 2019 also ask for two means inside the Spearman question, and in other years the grouped form of the same calculation opens the paper. The command word is Calculate, often with 'You must show your working'. Answers are given to 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise.
traps: Adding the values and squaring the total instead of squaring each value and adding (Summer 2019 Q3; the grouped form, the fx column squared, Summer 2019 Q1 and Summer 2024 Q1)
Stopping at the mean: about 30% earned only the mean's mark (Summer 2023 Q6)
Treating a table of days as grouped data, numbering the days, or dividing the sum of squares by the sum of the values (Summer 2025 Q2)
Giving the variance where the standard deviation was asked for, so the square root is missing
Using the calculator's $s_{x}$, which divides by $n - 1$, or giving a calculator answer with no working behind it
Rounding the mean to a whole number on the way, or chopping digits instead of rounding (Summer 2019 Q6)

noteBlocks.lede: Two shooters both average 12 goals a match. One scores 11, 12 or 13 every time; the other anything from 5 to 19. The mean cannot tell them apart. The standard deviation can: one number, in the data's own units, for how far the values typically sit from their mean.
can: Say which of two sets is more spread out, and why
Write $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$, squaring each value before adding
Work out the standard deviation of a list with the sheet's formula

noteBlocks.md: The mean says where a set of values sits. The standard deviation, written $\sigma$, says how tightly the values sit around that mean: roughly how far a typical value is from it. A small $\sigma$ means the values huddle; a large one means they scatter. It is in the units of the data, so a spread of goals is in goals.

noteBlocks.caption: Both shooters average 12 goals. P's standard deviation is 0.63 goals; Q's is 4.82 goals.

noteBlocks.stem: Over five matches Shooter P scored 11, 12, 13, 12 and 12 goals, and Shooter Q scored 5, 9, 12, 15 and 19. Compare their spreads.

steps.working: Both totals are 60, so $\bar{x} = 12$ for both
steps.decision: The means are equal, so the mean cannot separate the two shooters.

steps.working: P: every match is within 1 goal of 12
steps.decision: Read how far each value sits from the mean, not the values themselves.

steps.working: Q: 5 and 19 are each 7 goals from 12
steps.decision: Q's values sit much further from the mean than P's.
The standard deviation measures exactly that distance: 4.82 goals for Q against 0.63 for P.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two bus routes both average 20 minutes. Route A's five journeys take from 18 to 22 minutes; Route B's take from 9 to 31 minutes. Which route has the larger standard deviation?
options: Route B, with times from 9 to 31
Route A, with times from 18 to 22
They are equal, because the means are equal
noteBlocks.answer: Route B, with times from 9 to 31
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of See it, look at how far the values sit from the mean, not at the mean: Route B's journeys reach 11 minutes from 20, Route A's only 2. The standard deviation measures that distance, so Route B's is larger.

twin.prompt: Two ferries both average 40 minutes a crossing. Ferry T's five crossings take 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42 minutes; Ferry U's take 31, 36, 40, 44 and 49. Which ferry has the smaller standard deviation?
options: Neither: equal means give equal spreads
twin.explain: T's crossings are all within 2 minutes of 40, U's as far as 9 minutes away, so T's standard deviation is the smaller.

optionNotes.why: Ferry U's crossings sit as far as 9 minutes from the mean, so its spread is the larger.

optionNotes.option: Neither: equal means give equal spreads
optionNotes.why: The means match but the spreads do not; the standard deviation measures the spread alone.

optionNotes.option: Route A, with times from 18 to 22
optionNotes.why: Route A's times are the tightly packed ones, all within 2 minutes of 20, so its spread is the smaller.

optionNotes.option: They are equal, because the means are equal
optionNotes.why: Equal means say nothing about spread; telling such sets apart is the whole reason the standard deviation exists.

noteBlocks.caption: Each value is squared in its own column before anything is added.

noteBlocks.title: Why square at all?
noteBlocks.md: The distances of the values from their mean always add to zero: those above cancel those below. Squaring makes every distance count as positive, so they can be added without cancelling, and the square root at the end brings the answer back to the data's units.

noteBlocks.stem: Find $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$ for the values 3, 7, 9 and 10.

steps.decision: Add the values: no squaring yet.
Square every value on its own, in a second column.
Then add the squares. The total squared, $29^{2} = 841$, would be a different number altogether.

noteBlocks.prompt: For the values 6, 2 and 5, what is $\sum x^{2}$?
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of See it, square each value first, then add: $36 + 4 + 25 = 65$. Adding first and squaring the total, $13^{2} = 169$, gives $\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$ instead.

twin.prompt: For the values 2, 9 and 4, what is $\sum x^{2}$?
twin.explain: Square each value, then add: $4 + 81 + 16 = 101$. The total squared would be $15^{2} = 225$.

noteBlocks.text: A list: the formula in four steps

noteBlocks.md: Page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet prints $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \bar{x}^{2}}$. For a plain list each value counts once, so $f$ is 1, $\sum f$ is $n$, and the formula reads $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \bar{x}^{2}}$.
Work in four steps: the mean, because the formula needs it; $\sum x^{2}$, squaring first; the substitution; then the square root. The value under the root is the variance, and it is never negative.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the standard deviation of 4, 8, 9, 11 and 13.

steps.decision: Add the values and divide by $n = 5$: the formula needs the mean first.
Square each value, then add.
Substitute into the sheet's formula, with $\sum f$ read as $n$.
9.2 is the variance; its square root is the answer, to 2 decimal places.

noteBlocks.title: Standard deviation
noteBlocks.why: A Northern Ireland teacher working the Unit 3 formula on a list of values, step by step.

noteBlocks.prompt: Five values have a mean of 10 and $\sum x^{2} = 530$. What is their standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 3 and 4 of See it, substitute, then take the root: $\dfrac{530}{5} - 10^{2} = 6$, the variance, and $\sqrt{6} = 2.45$. Stopping at 6 would give the variance, not the standard deviation.

twin.prompt: Six values have a mean of 12 and $\sum x^{2} = 1000$. What is their standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: $\dfrac{1000}{6} - 12^{2} = 22.67$, the variance, and its square root is 4.76.

noteBlocks.text: A table of days is still a list

noteBlocks.md: A question may print its values in a table beside days of the week or names. Those are labels, not classes: there is nothing to take a midpoint of and nothing to number. Each entry is one value, so $n$ is the number of rows, and $\sum x^{2}$ is divided by $n$, never by $\sum x$.

noteBlocks.caption: Four values in a table: the days only label them.

noteBlocks.stem: A bus was late by 6 minutes on Monday, 11 on Tuesday, 3 on Wednesday and 8 on Thursday. Find the standard deviation of the four times.

steps.decision: The days only label the values: no midpoints, and no numbering the days 1 to 4.
Add the minutes and divide by the number of days.
Square each time, then add.
Divide $\sum x^{2}$ by $n$, the 4 days, not by $\sum x$; then take the root.

noteBlocks.prompt: A table gives the hours of sunshine on each of six days, Monday to Saturday. In the sheet's formula, what does $\sum f$ come to?
options: The sum of the six values
21, the days numbered 1 to 6 and added
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, the days only label the values, so each value counts once and $\sum f$ is $n$, here 6. The total of the values is $\sum x$, and numbering the days puts numbers in the formula that were never measured.

twin.prompt: A table gives the number of emails a teacher received on each of the 4 days she was in school. In the sheet's formula, what does $\sum f$ come to?
options: 10, the days numbered 1 to 4 and added
twin.explain: Each day's count is one value, so $\sum f$ is $n$: the 4 days.

optionNotes.why: That is $\sum x$, the total of the values; $\sum f$ counts how many values there are.

optionNotes.option: 10, the days numbered 1 to 4 and added
optionNotes.why: The days are labels, not data: numbering them invents values nobody measured.

optionNotes.option: The sum of the six values
optionNotes.why: That total is $\sum x$; dividing $\sum x^{2}$ by it is a slip examiners saw in 2025. $\sum f$ counts the values.

optionNotes.option: 21, the days numbered 1 to 6 and added
optionNotes.why: Numbering the days treats labels as data, which examiners saw in 2025; the days are only names for the values.

noteBlocks.md: In statistics mode you type the values once, and the calculator shows $\bar{x}$, $\sum x$, $\sum x^{2}$ and two deviations. $\sigma_{x}$ divides by $n$, as the sheet's formula does. $s_{x}$ divides by $n - 1$: a different quantity that this specification never asks for.

The paper still pays the working, and the 2025 report asked for calculator answers to be backed by it. Write $\sum x^{2}$, the substitution and then the value, so that a slip on the keys still leaves the method marks.

noteBlocks.stem: The four late-bus times, 6, 11, 3 and 8 minutes, are typed into a calculator in statistics mode.

steps.decision: The same totals as before: the calculator only saves the adding.
It divides by $n = 4$, so it agrees with the sheet's formula: 2.92.
It divides by $n - 1 = 3$: a different number, never asked for on this paper.
The working carries the method marks, even if a key is pressed wrongly.

noteBlocks.text: Keep the mean exact, round at the end

noteBlocks.md: Unless a question says otherwise, Unit 3 answers are given to 2 decimal places. That rounding happens once, at the end. A mean such as 10.75 goes into the formula exactly as it is: rounded to 11, it changes the variance, and the root can land a long way from the true value.

noteBlocks.title: Round once, never chop
noteBlocks.md: The 2019 report asked that means not be rounded to whole numbers, after marks were lost that way. The 2024 and 2025 reports asked for working values to carry more accuracy than the answer, and for the answer to be rounded, never cut short.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the standard deviation of 7, 10, 12 and 14.

steps.decision: Keep 10.75 exactly: it goes into the next line as it is.
Square first, then add.
Substitute with the exact mean.
Round once, at the end. With the mean rounded to 11 the root would be $\sqrt{1.25} = 1.12$, a different answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: Five values have $\sum x = 34$ and $\sum x^{2} = 250$. Keeping the mean exact, what is their standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: As in See it, keep the mean exact: $\bar{x} = 6.8$, so $\dfrac{250}{5} - 6.8^{2} = 3.76$ and $\sqrt{3.76} = 1.94$. Rounding the mean to 7 would give $\sqrt{1} = 1$.

twin.prompt: Four values have $\sum x = 29$ and $\sum x^{2} = 243$. Keeping the mean exact, what is their standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?

noteBlocks.md:
Say which of two sets is more spread out, from how far the values sit from the mean.
Write $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$, squaring each value before adding.
Work the four steps: the mean, $\sum x^{2}$, the substitution, the square root.
Treat a table of days as a plain list, with $n$ the number of values.
Use $\sigma_{x}$, keep the mean exact and round only the answer, to 2 decimal places.

Unit 3 sets this as a part of three to five marks (Summer 2023 Q6, Summer 2025 Q2), and most papers since 2019 ask for two means inside the Spearman question too. The first marks are for the mean and $\sum x^{2}$; the last is for the root, to 2 decimal places. Stuck: write the mean and $\sum x^{2}$, which earn marks on their own.

steps.decision: Count the values and add them. On a plain list every value counts once, so the sheet's $\sum f$ is just $n$.
The mean comes first because the standard-deviation formula needs it. Keep it exact; rounding here moves every later figure.
Square every value first, then add. This is a different number from $\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$, and mixing the two is the single most common way this question is lost.

options: $\sum x^{2}$ means square each value and then add, so it is 13614
$\sum x^{2}$ means add the values and then square, so it is 79524
$\sum x^{2}$ means square the mean, so it is 2209
whyMenu.explain: The sigma sits outside the square, so the squaring happens inside, value by value. Adding first and squaring gives 79524, which is far too large.

steps.decision: Substitute into the sheet's formula. The value under the root is the variance; it is never negative, so a negative here means the two squares have been swapped.
Take the square root last, and give it to 2 decimal places as the paper's front page asks. The variance 60 is not the answer.

On five Sundays the same warden counted 12, 18, 15, 21, 14 cars.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something from GCSE Mathematics: what is the mean of 6, 9, 12 and 13?
items.skill: The mean of a short list (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: $40 \div 4 = 10$. That division is the first line of every standard deviation.
That is the total. The mean divides it by how many values there are, here 4.
That is the middle of the list, the median. The mean adds the values and divides by how many there are.

items.stem: Before the lesson (new notation, so a guess is fine): what does the symbol $\sum$ tell you to do?

options.text: Add up everything that follows it
options.feedback: Yes. $\sum x$ adds the values; $\sum x^{2}$ adds their squares.

options.text: Multiply together everything that follows it
options.feedback: Not quite: $\sum$ only ever means add. A product has a different symbol.

options.text: Take the average of everything that follows it
options.feedback: Averaging is the division that comes after. $\sum$ is the adding on its own.

items.stem: Before the lesson, just a thought: two hockey teams both average 3 goals a match. What else would you want to know to compare them?
items.skill: Why an average is not the whole story

options.text: How spread out their scores are from match to match
options.feedback: Exactly the question this lesson answers, and the standard deviation is the number that answers it.

options.text: Nothing more: equal means make the teams equal
options.feedback: One team may score 3 every week and the other 0 then 6. The mean hides that; the spread shows it.
That does not change the scores. What separates the teams is how far their scores sit from the mean.

items.stem: For the values 3, 5, 8, what is $\sum x^{2}$?
items.skill: Square each value first, then add

options.feedback: That is $\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$: adding to 16 and then squaring. The sigma sits outside the square, so square first.
That is $\sum x$, with no squaring at all. The formula needs a second column of squares.

items.stem: A calculator in statistics mode shows both $\sigma_{x}$ and $s_{x}$. Which one does this specification's formula give?
items.skill: Choosing the divisor n rather than n minus 1

options.feedback: Yes. The sheet's formula has $\sum f$ underneath, which for a list of values is $n$.

options.text: $s_{x}$, because it is the more accurate one
options.feedback: $s_{x}$ divides by $n - 1$. It is a different quantity, and it is not what the sheet's formula produces.
They differ, and on a small data set they differ enough to lose the accuracy mark. Check which key you pressed.

items.stem: A pupil works out $\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \bar{x}^{2} = 4$ for a set of values. What is the standard deviation?
items.skill: Taking the square root as the final step

options.feedback: Yes. The bracket is the variance; the standard deviation is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
That is the variance, the number under the root. The formula finishes with a square root.
Squaring goes the wrong way. Rooting undoes the squaring that built the variance.

items.stem: A table lists five days of the week with the number of parcels delivered on each. Which is true?
items.skill: Telling raw values from grouped data

options.text: These are five raw values, so use $n = 5$ with no midpoints
options.feedback: Yes. The days are labels, not classes, so there is nothing to take a midpoint of.

options.text: The days are classes, so use midpoints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
options.feedback: Numbering the days invents data that was never collected. Examiners saw exactly this and it scored nothing.

options.text: The parcel counts are frequencies, so divide by their total
options.feedback: The counts are the data, not frequencies of something else. Ask what was measured before choosing the formula.

items.stem: A standard deviation works out as 5.6862 on the calculator. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Rounding to 2 decimal places without truncating

options.feedback: Yes. The paper asks for 2 decimal places, and the 6 in the third place rounds the 8 up.
That is the value chopped, not rounded: the 6 in the third place rounds the 8 up. Recent reports ask for rounding, never cutting digits off.
A whole number throws away accuracy the paper asks for: 2 decimal places is the default on Unit 3.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the variance. The last step of the formula is the square root, and $\sqrt{9.6} = 3.10$. The method mark for the substitution is safe; the working mark needs the root.
The five values were added and the total squared. $\sum x^{2}$ squares each value first, giving 293, not 1225. Rebuild the column of squares and the answer comes to 3.10.

In a choir, five singers each held one note for as long as they could. Their times were 31, 35, 36, 26 and 42 seconds.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$: the times were added and the total squared. Square each time first, then add; the column comes to 5922.

parts.stem: Hence calculate the standard deviation of the five times.
hints: Subtract the square of the mean, then take the root.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the variance, the number under the root. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{28.4} = 5.33$: the substitution mark is yours, the last mark needs the root.
The mean squared was never taken off, so the answer is the size of a time, not its spread. The method mark needs $\dfrac{5922}{5} - 34^{2}$ under the root.

parts.stem:
A cyclist timed her ride to school on six mornings. The times, in minutes, were 23, 31, 27, 35, 29 and 22.
Calculate the mean time.
hints: Divide by 6, and keep the answer to 2 decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: The mean has been rounded to a whole number. The total and the division earn the method mark; the answer needs 2 decimal places, 27.83.

parts.stem:
Calculate the standard deviation of the six times.
You must show your working.
hints: Subtract the square of the exact mean, then take the root.

commonErrors.feedback: The mean was rounded to 28 before it went into the formula. The sum of squares and the substitution are right, but the root needs the exact mean, 27.8333, and comes to 4.49.
That is the variance. The first two marks are yours; the last is for its square root, 4.49.
The mean squared was never taken off, so the answer is the size of a ride, not its spread. $\sum x^{2} = 4769$ earns its mark; subtract $27.8333^{2}$ under the root.
That divides by $n - 1$, as the calculator's $s_{x}$ does. $\sum x^{2} = 4769$ earns its mark; the sheet's formula divides by $n = 6$ and gives 4.49.
The six times were added and the total squared in place of $\sum x^{2}$. Square each time first; the column comes to 4769, and the answer to 4.49.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara was asked for the standard deviation of 21, 28, 25, 30, 16. Her working:
studentWorking: sd = square root of (14400 over 5 minus 24 squared) = 48.00
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 adds the values and squares the total. The sigma sits outside the square, so each value is squared first and the squares are added: 441 + 784 + 625 + 900 + 256 = 3006.
correction: sd = square root of (3006 over 5 minus 24 squared) = square root of 25.2 = 5.02
findTheMistake.feedback: The mean is right, so the first method-and-working mark is safe. The mark for $\sum x^{2}$ is lost at line 2 and it carries the rest of the question with it. Write a second column of squares beside the values before you add anything, and the standard deviation comes out as 5.02.

prompts.prompt: What does $\sum x^{2}$ tell you to do?
prompts.answer: Square each value, then add the squares.

prompts.answer: The standard deviation squared: the value under the root.

findings.asked: Mean and SD of a grouped frequency distribution.
findings.wentWrong: Mean fine; in the SD many squared the fx column rather than computing f x squared, and arithmetic slips were common.
findings.rule: The SD column is f times x squared, not (fx) squared.

findings.asked: Estimate mean and SD from grouped data.
findings.wentWrong: Some squared the sum of the fx column; arithmetic errors.
findings.rule: Compute sum fx and sum f x squared separately.

findings.asked: Mean and SD from a table of daily values.
findings.wentWrong: Some treated the table as grouped data and invented midpoints, or numbered the days 1 to 5; a sum was put into the formula in the wrong place; some scored nothing.
findings.rule: Identify whether the data are raw values or frequencies before choosing the formula.

findings.asked: The standard deviation of five marks, for 3 marks.
findings.wentWrong: About two thirds found it; about 30% earned only the mark for the mean.
findings.rule: Once the mean is down, write the sum of squares and substitute: each line is a mark.

insight.ruleToRemember: Mean = sum fx / sum f; SD from sum f x squared / sum f minus mean squared, then square root; check whether the table holds raw values or frequencies; keep full precision until the final rounding.
